title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night four: the list in the Devi Kavacha reaches Kushmanda, and in another way of keeping the festival, Durga's nights give way to Lakshmi's

segments.voice: Yesterday was night three of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum, the close of the first stretch of nights. What did you clear out of the way? Tonight the lesson turns. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

There's a short hymn called the Devi Kavacha, the goddess's armor, which some people recite before the Devi Mahatmya. Partway through, it counts the goddess out like stairs. First, Shailaputri. Second, Brahmacharini. Third, Chandraghanta. Fourth, Kushmanda. And on, name after name, until it says these are the nine Durgas. In some homes that list becomes the festival's calendar: one form of the goddess for each night. Tonight's name is Kushmanda. But there's a second way of keeping Navaratri, and it says something about tonight too. It gives the first three nights to Durga, the middle three to Lakshmi, and the last three to Saraswati. By that count, night four is a hinge.
screen: `THE DEVI KAVACHA COUNTS HER OUT.` → `FOURTH: KUSHMANDA.` → `NIGHT FOUR IS A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Start with Kushmanda. The Kavacha only names her; it doesn't tell her story. But there's a story people tell. Before anything existed there was only darkness, and the goddess smiled, and the world came out of that smile. Whatever you make of it, it's a bright picture to set on the fourth night: light that begins as a face lighting up. Now the second way of counting. The first three nights, Durga's, were the clearing nights. You can't plant a garden in a field full of rocks, so the curriculum starts by moving rocks. Then, on night four, Lakshmi arrives. Lakshmi is the goddess of good fortune, of plenty, of a household that has enough to share. Earlier this year, the Sri Sukta asked her to come and stay. The order matters. Clearing comes first, then filling. There's a homely version of this in some families: before welcoming Lakshmi, they clean the house, sweep the corners, light the lamp in a clean doorway. A guest like that, they say, comes to a room that's ready. So the fourth night of the curriculum asks a quieter question than the first three. The first nights asked what has to go. Tonight asks what you're making room for. Not more stuff. Enough. Health, a full table, friends at it, a little to give away. And the smile of Kushmanda sits over all of it, a reminder that in this story the good world begins with delight.
screen: `FOURTH NIGHT: KUSHMANDA.` · `A WORLD FROM A SMILE.` · `DURGA CLEARS, LAKSHMI FILLS.` · `WHAT ARE YOU MAKING ROOM FOR?` · then, large: `CLEARING FIRST, THEN FILLING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: making room. Settle, and let the breath slow. For the first stretch, notice the room you're sitting in: the space around you, the space above you, the quiet between sounds. Let it feel roomy. Then, for the second stretch, let one good thing into that room. A person you're grateful for. A meal you're glad of. Something already given. Let it sit there and be enough. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, quietly with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night four: Kushmanda in the Kavacha's list, and in the three-by-three way of counting, the night Lakshmi's nights begin.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, clear one small space, a shelf, a desk, a corner of the counter, and put one good thing there. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Some Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga named in the Devi Kavacha on each night of Navaratri; others, especially in parts of South India, give three nights each to Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati.

notes: Navaratri runs days 1109–1117 in the outline. This writer took 1109 = night one, so 1112 = night four, 1117 = night nine. If the 1109–1111 writer counted differently, the reviews and night numbers here need aligning.

The Devi Kavacha's Navadurga verses (Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda … Siddhidatri, 'nava durgah') are paraphrased; confirm the order and that 'the goddess's armor' is a fair gloss of Kavacha. Tradition attributes the Kavacha to the Varaha Purana; not stated.
Kushmanda's smile creating the world is told as 'a story people tell'; it comes from later Navadurga lore, not the Kavacha. Confirm.
The three-by-three Durga/Lakshmi/Saraswati scheme is described as one way of keeping the festival (howItsDone says 'especially in parts of South India'); confirm phrasing.
Cleaning the house to welcome Lakshmi is a Diwali custom; here it is offered as 'a homely version in some families'. Confirm it's fair to bring into Navaratri.
